examples.question_text: Find the value of $m$ for which $x^{2}-10x+5m=0$ has equal roots.
Find the values of $k$ for which $2x^{2}+6x+(k+1)=0$ has two distinct real roots.
examples.solution_text:
$a=2,\ b=6,\ c=k+1$.

Two distinct real roots require $\Delta>0$.

$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=6^{2}-4(2)(k+1)\\&=36-8k-8\\&=28-8k\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}28-8k&>0\\-8k&>-28\\k&<\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$

Dividing by $-8$ reverses the inequality.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $p$ for which $3x^{2}-8x+2p=0$ has no real roots.
examples.solution_text:
$a=3,\ b=-8,\ c=2p$.

No real roots require $\Delta<0$.

$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=(-8)^{2}-4(3)(2p)\\&=64-24p\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}64-24p&<0\\-24p&<-64\\p&>\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}$

Dividing by $-24$ reverses the inequality.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $2x^{2}+2(k+3)x+18=0$ has equal roots.
examples.solution_text:
$a=2,\ b=2(k+3),\ c=18$.

Equal roots require $\Delta=0$.

$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=[2(k+3)]^{2}-4(2)(18)\\&=4(k+3)^{2}-144\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}4(k+3)^{2}-144&=0\\(k+3)^{2}&=36\\k+3&=\pm6\\k&=-9\text{ or }3\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
For $x^{2}+px+49=0$, find the values of $p$ giving:

(a) two distinct real roots

(b) no real roots.
examples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=p,\ c=49$.

$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=p^{2}-4(1)(49)\\&=p^{2}-196\end{aligned}$

(a) Two distinct real roots require $\Delta>0$.

$\begin{aligned}p^{2}-196&>0\\(p+7\cdot2)(p-7\cdot2)&>0\end{aligned}$

The factors have the same sign when $p<-14$ or $p>14$.

(b) No real roots require $\Delta<0$.

$\begin{aligned}p^{2}-196&<0\\(p+14)(p-14)&<0\end{aligned}$

The factors have opposite signs when $-14<p<14$. At $p=\pm14$, the roots are equal, so both parts exclude these boundaries.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $(k-2)x^{2}+2(k-2)x+6=0$ has equal roots.
examples.solution_text:
When $k=2$, the equation becomes $6=0$, which has no solution. Hence $k\ne2$ is required for equal quadratic roots.

$a=k-2,\ b=2(k-2),\ c=6$.

Equal roots require $\Delta=0$.

$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=[2(k-2)]^{2}-4(k-2)(6)\\&=4(k-2)^{2}-24(k-2)\\&=4(k-2)(k-8)\end{aligned}$

$4(k-2)(k-8)=0$ gives $k=2$ or $k=8$.

Excluding $k=2$, the required value is $k=8$.

examples.derivation: Δ=100−20m. Equal roots require 100−20m=0, giving m=5. This adapts Solving equations Development Q8 using different values.
Δ=36−8(k+1)=28−8k. Two distinct real roots require 28−8k>0, giving k<7/2 after reversing the inequality when dividing by −8. This follows Development Q10.
Δ=64−4(3)(2p)=64−24p. No real roots require 64−24p<0, giving p>8/3. This follows Development Q11.
Δ=4(k+3)²−144. Setting Δ=0 gives (k+3)²=36, hence k=−9 or 3. The leading coefficient is always 2, so both values are permitted. This adapts Mastery Q13(b).

Δ=p²−196=(p+14)(p−14). It is positive for p<−14 or p>14 and negative for −14<p<14. At p=±14 it is zero, so both requested cases exclude the endpoints. The supplied discriminant rules and parameter exercises support this combination of retained assessed methods.

At k=2 the original equation is 6=0, so this value is excluded. Otherwise Δ=4(k−2)²−24(k−2)=4(k−2)(k−8). Setting Δ=0 leaves k=8 after exclusion; the resulting equation is 6(x+1)²=0. This follows the source's nonzero quadratic-coefficient condition and Mastery Q13(a).
